abstract: Ischaemic disease presents a significant challenge in medical science due to its widespread manifestations in the body and its tendency to only become overt in its late stages, beyond where current intervention methods are effective. Diseases such as coronary heart disease and peripheral artery disease (PAD) represent leading causes of death and are detrimental to quality of life. Focussing on the latter, PAD incurs an amputation rate of around 25%, largely owing to microvascular disease that prevents tissue recovery even after revascularisation. Current methods for investigating PAD either cannot chart specific vascular determinants, such as with in vivo imaging, or deform and remove subjects from longitudinal studies, such as with ex vivo tissue sampling. Presented to aid live research, computational modelling can collate information and build models of ischaemia using available information and provide a reasonable approximation of the disease's chronology and thus support understanding and advance research of PAD. Proposed here, is a 3D in silico model of ischaemic disease in the limb using a system of purpose-built platforms. Starting with a real micro-computed tomography image of the murine hindlimb, a realistic vessel bed was generated using vascular graphing software, ViGiL. From here, the model was realised in a defined pressure gradient via flow-modelling software, numPTI. With the base model of lower limb arteries, collateral vasculature was generated throughout the vessel space. This provides a bypass system for adaptation post-ischaemia. Upon ischaemic induction, the collateral bed responds to the loss of flow and successfully adapted to recover flow with similar density and distribution of diameters in collateral arterioles (p>> 0.05). Moreover, a satisfactory flow recovery of 50% was achieved after 6 days, showing that the model can reflect the specific vascular environment in which disease is incited. The proceeds of this study lay the groundwork for truly realistic ischaemic models including moving towards a predictive model than can signify when and where key indicators of PAD manifest.
